newsitem.title: Jordan: Jordan's Brotherhood calls for election boycott.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's Brotherhood calls for election boycott.

text.p: Jordan's powerful Moslem Brotherhood said on Wednesday it would boycott parliamentary elections due to be held in November.
The Brotherhood, whose Islamic Action Front (IAF) political arm is the country's largest parliamentary opposition party, said the decision was taken by its consultative council.
"The Moslem Brotherhood council decided to boycott the upcoming 1997 parliamentary elections," said a terse statement issued after a meeting late on Tuesday night.
But an IAF spokesman said the party needed time to study the boycott call.
"Personally I do not support boycotting. I am for participation," said IAF spokesman Hamza Mansour.
"I think the decision is a big one and a difficult one," Mansour told Reuters. "It will be studied, this decision, its effect and its dimensions on the election process."
The IAF, set up in 1992 when political parties were legalised, says it has no administrative or financial links with the Brotherhood.
But most of its members are Brotherhood members and all of its parliamentary deputies belong to the Brotherhood.
"If the Brotherhood members are committed to their decision then it will affect the Islamic Action Front," Mansour said.
Brotherhood head Abdul-Majid al-Thuneibat, who signed the boycott statement, said the movement would issue a detailed explanation of its decision later.

The elections are scheduled to be held by November this year but no date has been officially set. In the last elections in 1993 the Islamic Action Front won 16 of the 80 seats in a parliament filled with small pro-government parties and tribal representatives.

But it failed to block ratification of Jordan's 1994 peace treaty with Israel, which the Islamists want cancelled, and supporters of the boycott said it was time to pull out of a parliament which they said they could not influence.

"Even if there are (Islamist) parliamentary members they are weak because at least 60 deputies of the 80 represent the government," Islamist deputy Abdul-Moneim Abu Zunt said this week. He also said the elections might be rigged in favour of pro-government candidates.
Opponents of the boycott said that without parliamentary representation, the Islamists would lose their influence and their political party would become redundant.
They have said some Islamists would run as independent candidates if the IAF formally pulls out of the elections.
